You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Righteousness

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'righteousness' primarily denotes right standing before God and conformity to God's own moral character and standard. Its dominant theological use, especially in Protestant tradition, is the righteousness of God credited (imputed) to believers through faith in Christ rather than earned by works — often pictured symbolically as a clean or white garment/robe that covers the sinner. It thus functions both as a legal/relational status (justification) and as an ethical quality (upright living that flows from that status).",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Genesis 15:6 (Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness)",
    "Habakkuk 2:4 (the righteous shall live by faith)",
    "Romans 1:16-17; 3:21-26 (the righteousness of God revealed and given through faith in Christ)",
    "Romans 4:3-8 (righteousness counted apart from works)",
    "2 Corinthians 5:21 (that we might become the righteousness of God in him)",
    "Philippians 3:9 (a righteousness not my own, but through faith in Christ)",
    "Isaiah 61:10 (robe of righteousness); Isaiah 64:6 (our righteousnesses as filthy rags)",
    "Matthew 5:6, 5:20, 6:33 (hunger for righteousness; seek first God's kingdom and righteousness)",
    "Ephesians 6:14 (breastplate of righteousness)",
    "Revelation 19:8 (fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Forensic/imputed righteousness: a legal declaration in which Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer's account (classic Reformation/Protestant reading of justification).",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 4:3-8",
        "Romans 5:17-19",
        "2 Corinthians 5:21",
        "Philippians 3:9"
      ],
      "prominence": "dominant"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Infused/transformative righteousness: God's grace actually makes the believer inwardly righteous, so justification and sanctification are intertwined (Roman Catholic and Orthodox emphasis; Council of Trent).",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 5:5",
        "1 Corinthians 6:11",
        "James 2:21-24",
        "1 John 3:7 ('the one who practices righteousness is righteous')"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Ethical/behavioral righteousness: right conduct, integrity, and obedience to God's law as a lived moral quality, apart from any technical doctrine of justification (common in Old Testament wisdom and prophetic usage and in reading the Sermon on the Mount).",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 15",
        "Proverbs 10-15 (righteous vs. wicked contrasts)",
        "Ezekiel 18:5-9",
        "Matthew 5:20; 6:1"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Covenant faithfulness: 'the righteousness of God' as God's own faithfulness to his covenant promises, and human righteousness as covenant membership/loyalty (New Perspective on Paul: E.P. Sanders, James Dunn, N.T. Wright).",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 3:1-5, 3:25-26 (God's righteousness as his faithfulness/justice)",
        "Psalm 98:2-3",
        "Isaiah 46:13; 51:5-8 (righteousness paralleled with salvation and faithfulness)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Righteousness as social justice: tsedaqah/dikaiosyne understood chiefly as just treatment of the poor, the vulnerable, and society at large (liberation theology and some Old Testament scholarship; in later Jewish usage tsedaqah comes to mean almsgiving).",
      "basis": [
        "Amos 5:24 (let justice roll down... righteousness like an ever-flowing stream)",
        "Isaiah 1:16-17; 58:6-8",
        "Micah 6:8",
        "Jeremiah 22:3, 15-16"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Christological title: righteousness personified in or identified with Christ himself ('The LORD our righteousness'), so the term symbolizes Christ as the believer's righteousness.",
      "basis": [
        "Jeremiah 23:5-6; 33:16",
        "1 Corinthians 1:30 (Christ... our righteousness)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a genuine, widely recognizable consensus that righteousness centrally concerns right standing with God and conformity to his standard, with the garment/robe imagery (Isaiah 61:10; Revelation 19:8; cf. Zechariah 3:3-5) as its most common symbolic representation. The major fault line is not over the core meaning but over its mechanism: imputed (Protestant) vs. infused (Catholic/Orthodox) righteousness, plus the more recent scholarly debate over whether 'righteousness of God' means a status God gives or God's own covenant faithfulness (New Perspective). These are materially different but overlapping readings of a term whose lexical range (Hebrew tsedeq/tsedaqah; Greek dikaiosyne) spans legal, relational, ethical, and social-justice senses."
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "Moral and spiritual rightness before God: conformity to God’s character and will, including just conduct and, in salvation contexts, a right standing with God granted by grace.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Genesis 15:6 — Abraham’s faith is counted as righteousness.",
    "Psalm 106:3 — righteousness is associated with justice and right conduct.",
    "Isaiah 61:10 — salvation and righteousness are pictured as garments bestowed by God.",
    "Matthew 5:6, 10, 20 — righteousness characterizes those who seek and live under God’s reign.",
    "Matthew 6:33 — believers are to seek God’s kingdom and righteousness.",
    "Romans 1:16–17 — the gospel reveals the righteousness of God and connects it with faith.",
    "Romans 3:21–26 — righteousness is manifested through Christ and received through faith.",
    "Romans 4:3–8 — righteousness is counted apart from works.",
    "2 Corinthians 5:21 — believers become the righteousness of God in Christ.",
    "Philippians 3:8–9 — Paul contrasts righteousness based on law with righteousness through faith in Christ.",
    "Ephesians 6:14 — righteousness is symbolized as a protective breastplate."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "A forensic or judicial status: God declares the believer righteous because of Christ, often explained as Christ’s righteousness being imputed or credited to the believer.",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 3:21–28",
        "Romans 4:3–8",
        "Romans 5:17–19",
        "2 Corinthians 5:21",
        "Philippians 3:9"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "An imparted or transformative quality: grace actually makes a person righteous through sanctification, virtuous living, and participation in divine life, rather than righteousness being only a declared status.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 5:20",
        "Romans 6:13–19",
        "1 Corinthians 6:9–11",
        "James 2:14–26",
        "1 John 3:7"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Covenant faithfulness or covenant membership: righteousness denotes fidelity to covenant obligations, and justification identifies those recognized as members of God’s covenant people.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 15:6",
        "Deuteronomy 6:25",
        "Psalm 143:1–2",
        "Romans 3:1–6",
        "Galatians 2:15–21"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Justice and right social order, especially protection of the poor and oppressed; righteousness is closely paired with justice rather than treated primarily as private morality or individual salvation.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 72:1–4",
        "Isaiah 1:16–17, 21–27",
        "Isaiah 5:7",
        "Amos 5:24",
        "Matthew 25:31–46"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "God’s own saving justice and faithfulness: when Scripture speaks of the “righteousness of God,” it can signify God’s action in keeping promises, judging evil, and rescuing his people.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 98:1–3",
        "Isaiah 46:12–13",
        "Isaiah 51:5–8",
        "Romans 1:17",
        "Romans 3:25–26"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Christ himself as the believer’s righteousness: righteousness is interpreted christologically, with union with Christ being the source and embodiment of right standing and holy life.",
      "basis": [
        "Jeremiah 23:5–6",
        "1 Corinthians 1:30",
        "2 Corinthians 5:21",
        "Philippians 3:9"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad consensus on the core idea of rightness according to God—encompassing right standing, right conduct, and justice. There is no settled consensus across Christian traditions on whether saving righteousness is principally declared, imputed, imparted, covenantal, participatory, or some combination of these."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "Right standing with God (justification) and conformity to God's moral standards/will, often as a gift received by faith rather than earned by works",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Romans 3:21-26",
    "Romans 1:17",
    "Genesis 15:6",
    "Philippians 3:9",
    "2 Corinthians 5:21",
    "Matthew 5:6",
    "Matthew 6:33"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Personal moral uprightness, ethical conduct, or holy living produced in the believer",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 5:20",
        "1 John 3:7",
        "James 2:14-26",
        "Ephesians 4:24"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "God's own character of justice, faithfulness, and covenant loyalty (including God's saving acts)",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 11:7",
        "Psalm 89:14",
        "Isaiah 45:21-25",
        "Romans 3:25-26"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Social justice, equity, and righting of wrongs for the oppressed or poor",
      "basis": [
        "Amos 5:24",
        "Isaiah 1:17",
        "Micah 6:8",
        "Psalm 72:1-4"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Infused or transformative righteousness (inner renewal enabling good works) versus purely forensic/imputed status",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 5:5",
        "Titus 3:5-7",
        "Council of Trent canons on justification (historical Catholic framing)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Broad Christian consensus centers on right relationship with God and alignment with divine standards, with strong Pauline emphasis on righteousness as gift through faith. Denominational nuances (forensic imputation in much Protestant teaching vs. infused/transformative righteousness in Catholic and Orthodox traditions) and modern social-justice applications exist but do not overturn the primary forensic-relational and moral core attested across classic biblical interpretation."
}

BOOK ENTRY
The doing of God's commandments — the law kept, worn as the garment of righteous acts; not a vague goodness nor a verdict only received.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: right standing before God — Christ's imputed righteousness received by faith apart from works.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Deut 6:25; Ps 119:172; 1 John 3:7) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Deuteronomy 6:25 — And it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments before the LORD our God, as he hath commanded us.
Psalms 119:172 — My tongue shall speak of thy word: for all thy commandments are righteousness.
1 John 3:7 — Little children, let no man deceive you: he that doeth righteousness is righteous, even as he is righteous.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
